name: Cloud Composer
oneLiner: Managed Apache Airflow for orchestrating Google Cloud data workflows.
whatItIs: Cloud Composer is Google Cloud's managed Apache Airflow. Like MWAA on AWS, it runs standard Airflow — Python-defined DAGs, scheduler, workers, web UI — so you orchestrate pipelines without operating the infrastructure. It's tightly wired into GCP, with operators for BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataproc, Cloud Storage and more, so a DAG can say 'load to GCS, run a Dataflow job, then a BigQuery transform' and Composer will schedule and supervise it. It runs on GKE under the hood but you mostly interact with plain Airflow.

inPractice.narrative: A daily pipeline must land files in Cloud Storage, kick off a Dataflow job to process them, then run a BigQuery query to build a reporting table — in order, with retries and alerting. An engineer writes an Airflow DAG using GCP operators; Cloud Composer schedules it, runs each task against the right service, and shows the run in the Airflow UI. Composer conducts the pipeline; the actual work happens in Dataflow and BigQuery.

coreConcepts.detail: Python-defined directed acyclic graphs of tasks with dependencies — the same Airflow model as MWAA, versionable and dynamic.
Provider operators for BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataproc, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub and more let tasks drive GCP services directly.
Composer syncs DAG files and plugins from an associated Cloud Storage bucket into the environment — that's the deploy mechanism.
Composer 2 runs Airflow on autoscaling GKE with Workload Identity, scaling workers to load and improving cost/isolation over Composer 1.
You create a Composer environment (a managed Airflow deployment); sizing and node config determine capacity and cost.
Standard Airflow robustness: retry policies, sensors that wait for conditions, and backfilling historical runs.

whenToUse: Orchestrating multi-step GCP data pipelines in a defined order.
Teams wanting managed, standard open-source Airflow on GCP.
Coordinating BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataproc and GCS from one place.
Complex dependencies, retries, backfills and scheduling as Python code.
Portability of DAGs with other Airflow deployments.
whenNotToUse: Simple event-driven single-function triggers — Cloud Functions/Workflows are lighter.
Lightweight serverless step sequencing — Google Cloud Workflows may suffice.
Real-time/streaming flow — Airflow schedules batch, it isn't a stream processor.
Tiny/occasional needs where an always-on environment isn't cost-justified.

keyFacts.label: Engine
keyFacts.value: Managed Apache Airflow (Python DAGs) on GKE.

keyFacts.label: Role
keyFacts.value: Batch pipeline scheduling and dependency orchestration.

keyFacts.label: Deploy
keyFacts.value: DAGs synced from an associated Cloud Storage bucket.

keyFacts.label: Integrations
keyFacts.value: BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataproc, GCS, Pub/Sub operators.

pricingShape: Composer bills for the environment's underlying resources — the GKE compute, database and storage that run Airflow — for as long as the environment exists. Composer 2's autoscaling reduces worker cost at low load, but the scheduler/web components mean a baseline cost even when idle: an environment left running isn't free. As with MWAA, it's economical for steady orchestration and less so for rare or purely event-driven flows, where lighter Google Cloud Workflows/Functions may be cheaper.
gotchas: The environment runs continuously and bills even when no DAGs execute — plan for a baseline cost.
Python dependency/plugin conflicts are a frequent cause of broken environments — pin and test.
Composer 1 vs Composer 2 differ in architecture and cost model; use Composer 2 for new work.
Airflow orchestrates but doesn't process data — heavy lifting belongs in Dataflow/Dataproc/BigQuery.
Airflow/Composer version upgrades can break DAGs and providers; validate before upgrading prod.
